clue.text: Pudding poorly cooked — extremely lumpy

indicators.note: food that is cooked has been changed from its raw state, so the word before it is remade

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram material

indicators.note: extremely points to the two extremes, the outermost letters of the word that follows

parts.note: the first and last letters of lumpy

explanation.surface: A cook's complaint about a pudding that came out badly and full of lumps.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram takes both pieces together: all six letters of 'poorly' plus the two ends of 'lumpy'.
explanation.definitionFit: Roly-poly is a traditional British suet pudding rolled up with jam and steamed or baked.

clue.text: Murdoch to produce a comic strip?

definitions.note: the strip is named after its bear hero

parts.note: Rupert Murdoch, the media proprietor
to bear is to produce, as a tree bears fruit

explanation.surface: A press baron is set to launch a newspaper cartoon.
explanation.walkthrough: Murdoch owns newspapers that carry comic strips, so the surface sounds like business news.
explanation.definitionFit: Rupert Bear is the long-running Daily Express children's comic strip about a checked-trousered bear.

clue.text: The Parisian one certainly provides relaxation

parts.note: le is French for the
the Roman numeral for one
sure and certainly both affirm, as in 'sure, I'll come'

explanation.surface: A Parisian is said to know how to unwind.
explanation.definitionFit: Leisure is free time spent at rest or recreation, which is relaxation.

clue.text: Quietly go ahead and claim

parts.note: p is the musical marking piano, quietly
to lead is to go ahead of others

explanation.surface: An instruction to proceed discreetly and stake one's claim.
explanation.definitionFit: To plead is to assert or allege something, as in pleading ignorance, which is to claim it.

clue.text: Country line, the nicest possibly

indicators.note: possibly signals one possible arrangement among many, so the letters are reordered

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram material

explanation.surface: A claim that some national border or slogan is the nicest one around.
explanation.definitionFit: Liechtenstein is the small Alpine principality between Switzerland and Austria.

clue.text: King declared war — disastrously? Not entirely

indicators.note: not entirely tells us we use only part of the run of words before it, not all of them

parts.note: the letters run across the end of declared, all of war and the start of disastrously

explanation.surface: A monarch's declaration of war that went badly, though perhaps not completely.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer straddles three words: declarED WAR Disastrously.
explanation.definitionFit: Edward is the name of several English kings, from the Confessor to Edward VIII.

clue.text: Ring about Society girl's notice

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the first word goes round what follows

parts.note: to dial is to ring on the telephone
S is the abbreviation for society
a miss is a girl

explanation.surface: A phone call about a debutante's announcement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Society girl' reads as one phrase, a debutante; it splits into S and a young woman.
explanation.definitionFit: Notice in the sense of being given notice, a formal warning that one's job is ending, is dismissal.

clue.text: Sounds like a catch for a girl

indicators.note: sounds like tells us to go by how the words are spoken, not spelt

parts.note: a net is used to catch fish

explanation.surface: A fisherman's catch that someone thinks is a suitable present for a girl.
explanation.walkthrough: Spoken quickly, 'a net' runs together into the girl's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Annette is a female first name, so it fits a girl in crossword terms.

clue.text: A legal document, whichever way you look at it

indicators.text: whichever way you look at it
indicators.note: whichever way you look means the word reads the same from either end

parts.note: the word for this document is spelt identically backwards and forwards

explanation.surface: A legal paper that remains the same however you view it.
explanation.definitionFit: A deed is a written, signed and sealed instrument conveying property or rights.

clue.text: First of players to drive, having honour

indicators.note: first of asks for the opening letter only of the word that follows

parts.note: the opening letter of players
to ride is to drive or travel in a vehicle

explanation.surface: A golf picture: the leading player steps up to drive and is given the honour of going first.
explanation.walkthrough: In golf the 'honour' is the right to tee off first, which makes the surface sound like a definition-free sports report.
explanation.definitionFit: Pride and honour both name self-respect or a sense of one's own worth and dignity.

clue.text: Queen's lodged in Venice, surprisingly, from then till now

indicators.note: someone lodged in a place is housed inside it, so one piece sits within the other
surprisingly suggests the word appears in an unexpected form, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram material
ER, Elizabeth Regina, plus the 's

explanation.surface: The monarch has unexpectedly taken lodgings in Venice.
explanation.walkthrough: Venice is rearranged first to EVINCE, then ERS is lodged after its second letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Ever since is an adverbial phrase meaning continuously from a past moment up to the present.

clue.text: Remarkable run on old bicycle

parts.note: in cricket an extra is a run not scored off the bat
the penny-farthing was called an ordinary in Victorian times

explanation.surface: Someone rides an antique bicycle and is remarkable for it.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' puts the first piece above the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Extraordinary means beyond the ordinary, so very unusual or remarkable.

clue.text: Crazy about a dance popular in the 1960s

parts.note: round and about both mean around
the Twist was the dance craze launched by Chubby Checker

explanation.surface: Someone is mad about a sixties dance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crazy about' reads as one phrase meaning keen on; the split comes after 'Crazy'.
explanation.definitionFit: Round the twist is a British informal idiom for mad or insane.

clue.text: Holding on to old lady not saying a word

parts.note: keeping and holding on to are synonyms
old lady is slang for one's mother

explanation.surface: A carer holding an elderly woman's arm, in silence.
explanation.definitionFit: Keeping mum is a British idiom for staying silent and keeping a secret.

clue.text: Hairstyle popular in Utah?

parts.note: surface reading: a hairdo that is fashionable among people in Utah
setter's reading: the hairdo shares its name with Utah's state emblem, the symbol of industry chosen by its Mormon settlers

explanation.surface: A question about which hairdo is fashionable in Utah.
explanation.walkthrough: Utah's official nickname is the Beehive State, so the hive emblem is found everywhere there.
explanation.definitionFit: The beehive is a tall rounded bouffant hairstyle fashionable in the 1960s, shaped like a traditional straw hive.

clue.text: Elected soldier behind closed doors

parts.note: a candidate who is elected is in
a private is the lowest-ranking soldier

explanation.surface: A soldier voted into office meets in secret.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases describe something done secretly, away from public view.

clue.text: Severe south wind close to coastline

parts.note: Auster is the Latin name for the south wind

indicators.note: the close of a word is its end, so we keep only its last letter

parts.note: the final letter of coastline

explanation.surface: A harsh southerly gale blowing near the shore.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Close to coastline' reads as 'near the shore'; here close means the end of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Austere and severe both describe something stern, strict or plain without comfort.

clue.text: A rugby player, very large by the way

parts.note: taken as written
a prop is a front-row forward in rugby
OS stands for outsize, a clothing label for very large

explanation.surface: A passing remark that a certain rugby player is huge.
explanation.definitionFit: Apropos, used on its own, introduces a remark in passing, much like incidentally.

clue.text: Rest of English giving support to turbulent priest

indicators.note: turbulent means disturbed and unruly, so the following word's letters are thrown about

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram material
E for English, placed at the foot of a down answer to support the rest

explanation.surface: An English bishop backs a troublesome cleric, echoing Henry II on Becket.
explanation.walkthrough: Henry II's 'turbulent priest' was Thomas Becket.
explanation.definitionFit: A respite is a short break or pause from effort or difficulty, which is a rest.

clue.text: Hors d'oeuvre with portion of bread, and sponge to follow

parts.note: a roll is a small individual loaf
to mop is to sponge up, and to follow places it second

explanation.surface: A menu: a starter served with bread, then a sponge pudding for afters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sponge' pretends to be the cake for dessert; it is the verb, to wipe up.
explanation.definitionFit: A rollmop is a pickled herring fillet rolled around onion, served cold as a starter.

clue.text: Unit of explosive power — got name wrong

indicators.note: something wrong is out of its proper order, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram material

explanation.surface: Someone recorded the wrong name for a unit of explosive force.
explanation.definitionFit: A megaton measures explosive yield equal to a million tons of TNT, used for nuclear weapons.

clue.text: Comedian in lace factory I scold constantly? On the contrary

parts.note: to lace or spike a drink is to add alcohol or a drug to it
a mill is a factory, as in a cotton mill
taken as written

indicators.note: on the contrary means the opposite way round, so the last word is read back to front

parts.note: to nag is to keep scolding

explanation.surface: A worker in a lace factory complains about being told off all the time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lace' looks like the fabric made in the factory; it is the verb for doctoring a drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Spike Milligan was the Irish-born comedian and writer best known for The Goon Show.

clue.text: 18? Could get grant at university

definitions.note: refers to the answer at 18 down

parts.note: to let is to grant or allow
a student at university is said to be up

explanation.surface: A student wonders about getting a grant for university.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the cross-reference: 18 down is RESPITE.
explanation.definitionFit: A let-up is a pause or easing, the same as a respite or rest.

clue.text: All there over in Kinmel Bay

indicators.note: in a down answer over means turned upside down, so the letters run backwards
in tells us the letters are found inside the place name that follows

parts.note: the letters sit across the end of Kinmel and the start of Bay

explanation.surface: Someone is checking that everything is present in a North Wales seaside town.
explanation.walkthrough: Kinmel Bay is a resort in North Wales; the letters straddle its two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Being all there means mentally alert, and an able person is competent and capable.

clue.text: Female figure in Rabat in assassination

indicators.note: an assassination destroys and breaks things apart, so the letters before it are reassembled

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram material

explanation.surface: A woman is caught up in a killing in the Moroccan capital.
explanation.walkthrough: Both small words around Rabat look like link words; they are part of the fodder. Rabat is the capital of Morocco.
explanation.definitionFit: Britannia is the helmeted female personification of Britain, shown with trident and shield on coins.

clue.text: Pole maiden has to carry at the front

parts.note: to tote is to carry, and at the front places it before the next piece
M is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for a maiden over

explanation.surface: A Polish young woman has to lead the way carrying something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pole' with its capital looks like a Polish person; it is the carved post, a totem standing by extension for the totem pole.
explanation.definitionFit: A totem is the carved emblem on a totem pole, so the word stands for the pole itself.

clue.text: Soccer team finding time for a drink?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a football side has this many players
second meaning: the hour of the mid-morning tea or coffee break

explanation.surface: A football side looks for a moment to go for a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: Elevenses is the British mid-morning snack or cuppa, taken around this hour.
explanation.definitionFit: A football side is called an eleven from its number of players; eleven o'clock is elevenses time.

clue.text: Drum major's beginning to get in my punt — a lunatic

indicators.note: lunatic means crazy, so the letters go wild and are rearranged
a word's beginning is its first letter, so only that is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of major
taken as written, as anagram material

explanation.surface: A drum major climbs into someone's punt, and the boat's owner is a madman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drum major' reads as one title; the split leaves 'Drum' as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The tympanum is the eardrum, and also a term for a drum or drumhead.
